questions.question: The system of equations \[\begin{aligned} x + y + z &= 6 \\ x + 4y + 6z &= 20 \\ x + 4y + \lambda z &= \mu \end{aligned}\] has NO solution for values of \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) given by
questions.explanation:
Given \(AX = B\). \[[A|B] = egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & ig| & 6 \ 1 & 4 & 6 & ig| & 20 \ 1 & 4 & \lambda & ig| & \mu \end{pmatrix}\] Step 1: \(R_{2} ightarrow R_{2} - R_{1}\) and \(R_{3} ightarrow R_{3} - R_{1}\): \[[A|B] \sim egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & ig| & 6 \ 0 & 3 & 5 & ig| & 14 \ 0 & 3 & \lambda - 1 & ig| & \mu - 6 \end{pmatrix}\] Step 2: \(R_{3} ightarrow R_{3} - R_{2}\): \[[A|B] \sim egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & ig| & 6 \ 0 & 3 & 5 & ig| & 14 \ 0 & 0 & \lambda - 6 & ig| & \mu - 20 \end{pmatrix}\] The system has no solution if the rank of the coefficient matrix \(A\) is not equal to the rank of the augmented matrix \([A|B]\) (\( ho(A) eq ho[A|B]\)). This condition occurs when:
  • \(\lambda - 6 = 0 \implies \lambda = 6\) (This makes \( ho(A) = 2\))
  • \(\mu - 20 eq 0 \implies \mu eq 20\) (This makes \( ho[A|B] = 3\))
Under these conditions, \( ho(A) = 2 eq 3 = ho[A|B]\). Therefore, the system has no solution if \(\lambda = 6\) and \(\mu eq 20\). \[ oxed{ ext{(B) $\lambda = 6$, $\mu eq 20$}}\]
Key points
  • Consistency Criteria:
    • Unique Solution: \( ho(A) = ho[A|B] = n\) (number of variables).
    • Infinite Solutions: \( ho(A) = ho[A|B] < n\).
    • No Solution: \( ho(A) eq ho[A|B]\).

questions.question: A numerical solution of the equation \(f(x) = x + \sqrt{x} - 3 = 0\) can be obtained using Newton-Raphson method. If the starting value is \(x = 2\) for the iteration, then the value of \(x\) that is to be used in the next step is
questions.explanation:
We are given the function: \[f(x) = x + \sqrt{x} - 3 = 0\] Differentiating with respect to \(x\) yields: \[f'(x) = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\] We are given the initial starting value \(x_0 = 2\). We need to compute the next step value \(x_1\) using the Newton-Raphson formula. Step 1: Evaluate \(f(x)\) and \(f'(x)\) at \(x_0 = 2\) \[f(2) = 2 + \sqrt{2} - 3 = \sqrt{2} - 1 \approx 1.414213 - 1 = 0.414213\] \[f'(2) = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \approx 1 + \dfrac{1}{2(1.414213)} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2.828427} \approx 1 + 0.353553 = 1.353553\] Step 2: Calculate \(x_1\)
\[x_1 = x_0 - \dfrac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)} = 2 - \dfrac{0.414213}{1.353553} \approx 2 - 0.306019 = 1.69398\] The value closest to our result among the options is \(1.694\) (Option C). However, checking the literal parameter wording "the value of \(x\) that is to be used in the next step is...", if it refers to the modification offset term \(-\dfrac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)} \approx -0.306\), or if the question text maps to \(x_1 = 2.306\) via alternative matching indices, let us verify the full root value: \[x_1 \approx 1.694\] \[\boxed{\text{C. 1.694}}\]
Key points
  • Radical Differentiation: Always apply the power rule carefully when taking derivatives of fractional radicals: \[\frac{d}{dx}(x^{1/2}) = \frac{1}{2}x^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\]

questions.question: In the circuit shown below, the initial charge on the capacitor is \(2.5\text{ mC}\), with the voltage polarity as indicated. The switch is closed at time \(t = 0\). The current \(i(t)\) at a time '\(t\)' after the switch is closed is
questions.explanation:
Method Transient Analysis
The capacitor current is given by, \(i(t) = i(\infty) + \left[i(0^+)-i(\infty)\right] e^{-t/\tau}\) The initial capacitor voltage is \[Q = CV\] \[2.5~\text{mC} = 50~\mu\text{F}\times V_C(0^-)\] \[V_C(0^-) = \frac{2.5\times10^{-3}}{50\times10^{-6}} = 50~\text{V}\] Since capacitor voltage is continuous, \(\Rightarrow V_C(0^+)=50~\text{V}\) At \(t=0^+\), the capacitor is replaced by its initial voltage source. Applying KVL, \[-100+10\,i(0^+)-50=0\] \[i(0^+) = \frac{100+50}{10} = 15~\text{A}\] For the RC circuit, \[\tau = RC = 10\times50\times10^{-6} = 5\times10^{-4}~\text{s}\] At steady state, the capacitor behaves as an open circuit, \(\Rightarrow i(\infty)=0\) Hence, \[i(t) = 15e^{-t/(5\times10^{-4})} = 15e^{-2\times10^3t}\ \text{A}\]
Method Option Elimination
At \(t=0^+\), the capacitor is replaced by its initial voltage source of \(50~\text{V}\). Applying KVL, \[-100+10\,i(0^+)-50=0\] \[i(0^+)=15~\text{A}\] From the options, \[\text{(A)} \Rightarrow i(0^+)=15~\text{A}, \quad \text{(B)} \Rightarrow i(0^+)=5~\text{A}, \quad \text{(C)} \Rightarrow i(0^+)=10~\text{A}, \quad \text{(D)} \Rightarrow i(0^+)=-5~\text{A}\] Matching with options, we get option A. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }15e^{-2\times10^3t}\ \text{A}}\]

questions.question: The circuit shown below is driven by a sinusoidal input \(v_i = V_p\cos(t/RC)\). The steady state output \(v_o\) is
questions.explanation: For any sinusoidal input passing through an LTI (Linear Time-Invariant) system with a transfer function \(G(s)\), the steady-state output response \(V_o(j\omega)\) is given by: \[V_o(j\omega) = |V_i(j\omega)| \cdot |G(j\omega)| \angle \big(\angle V_i(j\omega) + \angle G(j\omega)\big)\] First, let us determine the transfer function \(G(s)\) of the system using s-domain analysis. The parallel combination in the circuit is given by: \[\frac{1}{Cs} \parallel R = \frac{\frac{1}{Cs} \cdot R}{\frac{1}{Cs} + R} = \frac{R}{RCs + 1}\] Using the voltage divider rule, the transfer function \(G(s) = \frac{V_o(s)}{V_i(s)}\) is expressed as: \[G(s) = \frac{\frac{1}{Cs} \parallel R}{R + \frac{1}{Cs} + \left(\frac{1}{Cs} \parallel R\right)}\] \[G(s) = \frac{\frac{R}{RCs + 1}}{R + \frac{1}{Cs} + \frac{R}{RCs + 1}}\] Multiplying the numerator and the denominator by \((RCs + 1)\): \[G(s) = \frac{R}{\left(R + \frac{1}{Cs}\right)(RCs + 1) + R}\] \[G(s) = \frac{R}{R^2Cs + R + R + \frac{1}{Cs} + R}\] Multiplying the numerator and the denominator by \(Cs\) to eliminate the fraction: \[G(s) = \frac{RCs}{R^2C^2s^2 + 3RCs + 1}\] To find the frequency response, substitute \(s = j\omega\): \[G(j\omega) = \frac{jRC\omega}{(j\omega)^2 R^2C^2 + 3jRC\omega + 1} = \frac{jRC\omega}{-\omega^2 R^2C^2 + 3jRC\omega + 1}\] Given the operating frequency is \(\omega = \frac{1}{RC}\). Substituting \(\omega\) into the frequency response equation: \[\left. G(j\omega) \right|_{\omega = \frac{1}{RC}} = \frac{j \cdot (1)}{-\left(\frac{1}{RC}\right)^2 R^2C^2 + 3j \cdot (1) + 1}\] \[\left. G(j\omega) \right|_{\omega = \frac{1}{RC}} = \frac{j}{-1 + 3j + 1} = \frac{j}{3j} = \frac{1}{3}\] Evaluating the magnitude and phase of the transfer function at this frequency: \[|G(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{3}, \quad \angle G(j\omega) = 0^\circ\] Thus, we can conclude that the amplitude of the output voltage is scaled to \(\frac{1}{3}\text{rd}\) of the input amplitude, and the phase difference between the output and input is zero. Assuming an input voltage of \(V_p \cos(\omega t)\), the time-domain output voltage \(V_o(t)\) is: \[V_o(t) = \frac{V_p}{3} \cos\left(\frac{t}{RC}\right)\] \[\boxed{(a) (V_p/3) \cos(t/RC)}\]

questions.question: A system is defined by its impulse response \(h(n) =2^n u(n - 2)\). The system is
questions.explanation:
\[h(n) = 2^n u(n - 2)\] For causal system \(h(n) = 0\) for \(n < 0\) Hence given system is causal. For stability: \(\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} 2^n = \infty\), so given system is not stable. \[\boxed{\text{B) causal but not stable}}\]
Key points
  • Causality: A discrete-time LTI system is causal if its impulse response satisfies \(h(n) = 0\) for all \(n < 0\). The presence of \(u(n-2)\) ensures \(h(n)\) is zero for \(n < 2\), fulfilling this condition.
  • Stability: A discrete-time LTI system is bounded-input bounded-output (BIBO) stable only if its impulse response is absolutely summable: \(\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |h(n)| < \infty\). An exponentially growing function like \(2^n\) will diverge, making the system unstable.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume a system is non-causal just because of a time-shifted step function. A delay (\(n-2\)) keeps the non-zero values in the positive time domain (\(n \ge 2\)).
  • Be careful to evaluate the summation bounds correctly. The unit step \(u(n-2)\) changes the lower limit of the summation from \(-\infty\) to \(2\).

questions.question: The trigonometric Fourier series of an even function does not have the
questions.explanation:
A periodic signal \(f(t)\) can be represented by its trigonometric Fourier series as: \[f(t) = a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left[ a_n \cos(n\omega_0 t) + b_n \sin(n\omega_0 t) \right]\] For an even function, the condition \(f(t) = f(-t)\) holds true. The coefficient for the sine terms, \(b_n\), is evaluated over a symmetric period \(T_0\) as: \[b_n = \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-T_0/2}^{T_0/2} f(t) \sin(n\omega_0 t) \, dt\] Since \(f(t)\) is an even function and \(\sin(n\omega_0 t)\) is an odd function, their product \(f(t)\sin(n\omega_0 t)\) results in an odd function. The definite integral of an odd function evaluated over a symmetrical interval \([-T_0/2, T_0/2]\) is always zero. \[\implies b_n = 0\] Therefore, the trigonometric Fourier series of an even function consists only of the DC term (\(a_0\)) and cosine terms (\(a_n\)). It does not contain sine terms. \[\boxed{\text{C) sine terms }}\]
Key points
  • Even Symmetry: If \(f(t) = f(-t)\), the Fourier series contains only DC and cosine terms (\(b_n = 0\)).
  • Odd Symmetry: If \(f(t) = -f(-t)\), the Fourier series contains only sine terms (\(a_0 = 0, a_n = 0\)).
  • Half-Wave Symmetry: If \(f(t) = -f(t \pm T_0/2)\), the Fourier series contains only odd harmonics (coefficients for even \(n\) are zero).

questions.question: If \(F(s) = L[f(t)] = \frac{2(s+1)}{s^2+4s+7}\) then the initial and final values of \(f(t)\) are respectively
questions.explanation:
\[F(s) = L[f(t)] = \frac{2(s + 1)}{s^2 + 4s + 7}\] Initial value, \[\lim_{t \to 0} f(t) = \lim_{s \to \infty} sF(s) = \lim_{s \to \infty} s \cdot \frac{2(s + 1)}{s^2 + 4s + 7}\] \[= \lim_{s \to \infty} \frac{2s^2 \left(1 + \frac{1}{s}\right)}{s^2 \left(1 + \frac{4}{s} + \frac{7}{s^2}\right)}\] \[= \frac{2(1 + 0)}{(1 + 0 + 0)} = 2\] Final value, \[\lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} sF(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot \frac{2(s + 1)}{s^2 + 4s + 7}\] \[= 0\] \[\boxed{B) 2, 0}\]
Key points
  • Initial Value Theorem: \(\lim_{t \to 0} f(t) = \lim_{s \to \infty} sF(s)\)
  • Final Value Theorem: \(\lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} sF(s)\)

questions.question: The first six points of the 8-point DFT of a real valued sequence are \(5, 1 - j3, 0, 3- j4, 0\) and \(3+ j4\). The last two points of the DFT are respectively
questions.explanation:
For a real-valued sequence \(x[n]\), its \(N\)-point Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), denoted as \(X[k]\), exhibits conjugate symmetry. This property is mathematically expressed as: \[X[k] = X^*[N - k]\] for \(k = 1, 2, \dots, N-1\). Given a sequence length of \(N = 8\), the first six points of the DFT sequence are provided as: \[X[0] = 5\] \[X[1] = 1 - j3\] \[X[2] = 0\] \[X[3] = 3 - j4\] \[X[4] = 0\] \[X[5] = 3 + j4\] We are required to find the last two points of the 8-point DFT, which correspond to the indices \(k = 6\) and \(k = 7\). Applying the conjugate symmetry property for \(k = 6\): \[X[6] = X^*[8 - 6] = X^*[2]\] Substituting the given value of \(X[2] = 0\): \[X[6] = 0^* = 0\] Similarly, applying the property for \(k = 7\): \[X[7] = X^*[8 - 7] = X^*[1]\] Substituting the given value of \(X[1] = 1 - j3\): \[X[7] = (1 - j3)^* = 1 + j3\] Thus, the last two points of the DFT are \(0\) and \(1 + j3\), which matches Option B. \[\boxed{\text{B) $0, 1+ j3$}}\]
Key points
  • For a purely real sequence in the time domain, its frequency domain representation (DFT) is conjugate symmetric.
  • The conjugate symmetry relationship is given by \(X[k] = X^*[N-k]\).
  • For an even number of points \(N\), the components at \(X[0]\) (DC component) and \(X[N/2]\) (Nyquist frequency) are always purely real.
Mistakes to avoid
A common mistake is incorrectly identifying the folding index. The symmetry for an \(N\)-point DFT is defined such that index \(k\) pairs directly with \(N-k\). For an 8-point sequence, do not pair \(X[1]\) with \(X[6]\); always verify the folding symmetry around the Nyquist point \(N/2 = 4\).

questions.question: Drift current in the semiconductors depends upon
options: both the electric field and the carrier concentration
both the electric field and the carrier concentration gradient
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Drift current density is defined as \(J_{drift} = \sigma E\), where \(\sigma\) is the conductivity and \(E\) is the electric field. Since conductivity depends on the carrier concentration (\(\sigma = qn\mu_{n} + qp\mu_{p}\)), the drift current depends on both the electric field and the carrier concentration.
Method 2
The drift current density can also be expressed as \(J_{drift} = qnv_{d}\), where \(v_{d}\) is the drift velocity. Because drift velocity is directly proportional to the electric field (\(v_{d} = \mu E\)), the total current is a function of both the carrier concentration (\(n\)) and the electric field (\(E\)).
\[\boxed{(C) \text{ both the electric field and the carrier concentration}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse drift current with diffusion current; diffusion current depends on the concentration gradient, not the electric field directly.

questions.question: A Zener diode, when used in voltage stabilization circuits, is biased in
options: reverse bias region below the breakdown voltage
questions.explanation:
In the forward bias region, the diode conducts once the barrier potential is overcome. In the reverse bias region, the diode remains non-conductive (behaving like an open circuit) until the reverse voltage reaches the breakdown threshold. [figure unavailable]
  • Reverse Bias Region (Below Breakdown): Here, the current is negligible (leakage current), effectively behaving as an open circuit.
  • Breakdown Region: Beyond the breakdown voltage , the current increases sharply. This is the region where Zener diodes are specifically designed to operate for voltage regulation.
\[\boxed{(B) \text{ reverse breakdown region}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure you distinguish between the "Reverse Bias Region" (low current) and the "Breakdown Region" (high current).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: A silicon PN junction is forward biased with a constant current at room temperature. When the temperature is increased by \(10^{\circ}\,\text{C}\), the forward bias voltage across the PN junction
questions.explanation:
The temperature dependence of the forward voltage (\(V\)) across a p-n junction diode under a constant forward current is characterized by a negative temperature coefficient. The rate of change of voltage with respect to temperature is given by: \[\frac{dV}{dT} = -2.5\,\text{mV/}^\circ\text{C}\] For a temperature increase of \(\Delta T = 10\,^\circ\text{C}\), the change in forward voltage (\(\Delta V\)) can be calculated as: \[\Delta V = \frac{dV}{dT} \times \Delta T\] \[\Delta V = -2.5\,\text{mV/}^\circ\text{C} \times 10\,^\circ\text{C} = -25\,\text{mV}\] The negative sign indicates that the voltage decreases. Therefore, the voltage across the p-n junction will decrease by \(25\,\text{mV}\). \[\boxed{(D) \text{ decreases by 25 mV}}\]
Key points
  • The forward voltage of a silicon diode decreases by approximately \(2\,\text{mV}\) to \(2.5\,\text{mV}\) for every \(1\,^\circ\text{C}\) increase in temperature.
  • This negative temperature coefficient occurs because the intrinsic carrier concentration \(n_{i}\) increases exponentially with temperature, which significantly increases the reverse saturation current \(I_{s}\) and consequently lowers the required forward bias voltage for a given current.

questions.question: For a BJT the common base current gain \(\alpha = 0.98\) and the collector base junction reverse bias saturation current \(I_{CO} = 0.6\,\mu\text{A}\). This BJT is connected in the common emitter mode and operated in the active region with a base drive current \(I_B = 20\,\mu\text{A}\). The collector current \(I_C\) for this mode of operation is
questions.explanation: The collector current of a BJT including leakage is: \[I_C = \beta I_B + (1 + \beta)I_{CO}\] Converting the given common-base current gain to common-emitter current gain: \[\beta = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha} = \frac{0.98}{1 - 0.98} = \frac{0.98}{0.02} = 49\] Substituting values: \[I_C = 49 \times 20 + (1 + 49) \times 0.6 = 1.01\,\text{mA}\] \[\boxed{(D)\, 1.01\,\text{mA}}\]

questions.question: For a BJT, the common-base current gain \(\alpha = 0.98\) and the collector base junction reverse bias saturation current \(I_{CO} = 0.6 \mu\text{A}\). This BJT is connected in the common emitter mode and operated in the active region with a base drive current \(I_B = 20 \mu\text{A}\). The collector current \(I_C\) for this mode of operation is
questions.explanation:
Given \(I_s = 0.6\,\mu\text{A}\), \(\alpha = 0.98\) and \(I_B = 20\,\mu\text{A}\) Current gain \(\beta\) is given as: \[\beta = \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\] \[\beta = \frac{0.98}{1-0.98} = 49\] Collector current in terms of reverse bias saturation current is given as: \[I_C = \beta I_B + (1 + \beta)I_s\] \[I_C = 49 \times 20\,\mu\text{A} + (50) \times 0.6\,\mu\text{A}\] \[I_C = 0.98\,\text{mA} + 0.03\,\text{mA} = \boxed{1.01\,\text{mA}}\]
Key points
  • The relationship between the common-base current gain (\(\alpha\)) and the common-emitter current gain (\(\beta\)) is \(\beta = \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\).
  • The total collector current \(I_C\) in active mode accounts for both the amplified base current and the leakage current, given by \(I_C = \beta I_B + (1 + \beta)I_{CO}\), where \(I_{CO}\) (or \(I_s\)) is the reverse saturation current of the collector-base junction.

questions.question: In the circuit shown below, capacitors \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are very large and are shorts at the input frequency. \(v_i\) is a small signal input. The gain magnitude \(|v_o/v_i|\) at \(10 \text{ Mrad/s}\) is
questions.explanation:
Given operating frequency is 10Mrad/sec and given circuit is, For the parallel RLC circuit, the resonant frequency is \[\omega_r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10 \times 10^{-6} \times 1 \times 10^{-9}}} = 10\,\text{Mrad/sec}\] So the given circuit is in resonance and at resonance the impedance of parallel RLC is maximum and purely resistive \(= Z_{\text{max}} = R = 2\,\text{k}\Omega\) The given circuit is a common emitter amplifier with emitter bypass capacitor whose gain is \[A_V= -g_m (Z_C \parallel R_L)\] Since \(Z_C\) is maximum , the gain is also maximum. \[\boxed{\text{(A)\quad maximum}}\]
Key points
  • At resonance, the impedance of a parallel RLC tank circuit is purely resistive and reaches its maximum value, which is equal to the parallel resistance \(R\).
  • Because the magnitude of the amplifier's voltage gain is directly proportional to the load impedance (\(|A_v| \approx g_m |Z_{\text{load}}|\)), the gain attains its maximum value at the resonant frequency.

questions.question: For the BJT \(Q_1\) in the circuit shown below, \(\beta = \infty\), \(V_{BEon} = 0.7 \text{ V}\), \(V_{CEsat} = 0.7 \text{ V}\). The switch is initially closed. At time \(t=0\), the switch is opened. The time \(t\) at which \(Q_1\) leaves the active region is
questions.explanation:
Given, \(\beta\) is very large, hence \(I_B = \frac{I_C}{\beta} = \frac{I_C}{\infty} = 0\,\text{A}\) and therefore \(I_C \approx I_E\), \(V_{BE(\text{ON})} = 0.7\,\text{V}\), \(V_{CE(\text{sat})} = 0.7\,\text{V}\). Given circuit is shown below, From figure, \(-10\,\text{V}\) is more negative as compared to \(-5\,\text{V}\). Therefore, input junction is in forward bias. Applying KVL in input loop, \[5 + 0.7 + 4.3 \times I_C - 10 = 0\] \[4.3 I_C = 4.3\] \[I_C = 1\,\text{mA}\] At \(t = 0^-\) , switch is closed. Capacitor voltage \(V_C(0^-) = 0\,\text{V}\). Collector voltage \(V_C = 0\,\text{V}\) Note : \(I_C = 1\,\text{mA}\) is fixed because other elements are fixed, which are responsible for current \(I_C\). Applying KVL in loop (2), \[-V_C + V_{CE} + 4.3 \times 1 - 10 = 0\] \[V_C = V_{CE} + 4.3 \times 1 - 10\] \[0 = V_{CE} + 4.3 \times 1 - 10\] \[V_{CE} = 5.7\,\text{V}\] \[V_{CB} = V_{CE} - V_{BE} = 5.7 - 0.7 = 5\,\text{V}\] Since the collector is n-type and \(V_{CB}\) is positive, collector junction is in reverse bias. Hence at \(t = 0^-\) given transistor is in active region. At \(t = 0\) , switch is opened. From above figure, \(V_C(t) = V_{Cap}(t)\) Applying KCL at collector terminal, \[-0.5 + I_{Cap} + 1 = 0\] \[0.5 = I_{Cap} + 1\] \[I_{Cap} = -0.5\,\text{mA} \quad [\text{Constant value}]\] Here, capacitor will linearly charge in opposite direction or linearly discharge. Capacitor voltage is given by, \[V_{Cap}(t) = \frac{1}{C} \int_{0}^{t} I_{Cap}(t) dt\] \[V_{Cap}(t) = \frac{1}{5 \times 10^{-6}} \int_{0}^{t} -0.5 \times 10^{-3} dt\] \[V_{Cap}(t) = -100t \quad \dots \text{(i)}\] When transistor enters into saturation region, \[V_{CE(\text{sat})} = 0.7\,\text{V} \quad [\text{Given}]\] From figure, \[V_{Cap}(t) = V_{CE} + I_C R_E - 10\] \[V_{Cap}(t) = 0.7 + 1 \times 4.3 - 10\] \[V_{Cap}(t) = -5\,\text{V} \quad \dots \text{(ii)}\] Equating equation (i) and (ii), \[-5 = -100 \times t\] \[t = \frac{5}{100} = 0.05\,\text{sec} = 50\,\text{msec}\] Upto \(50\,\text{msec}\) transistor is in active region. After \(50\,\text{msec}\) transistor leaves the active region and goes to saturation region. \[\boxed{\text{(C)\quad 50 ms}}\]
Key points
  • If instead of \(-10\,\text{V}\), \(R_E\) was connected to ground, then emitter base junction would be in reverse bias. Proper biasing ensures initial operation in the active region.
  • A constant current flowing out of a capacitor node causes the capacitor voltage to decrease linearly with time according to \(V(t) = \frac{I}{C}t\).
  • The boundary of the active region occurs when the collector-emitter voltage drops to \(V_{CE(\text{sat})}\). By substituting \(V_{CE} = V_{CE(\text{sat})}\) into the KVL equation, the corresponding collector voltage and the time it takes to reach it can be determined.

questions.question: The output \(Y\) in the circuit below is always ``1'' when
options: two or more of the inputs \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\) are ``0''
two or more of the inputs \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\) are ``1''
any odd number of the inputs \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\) is ``0''
any odd number of the inputs \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\) is ``1''
questions.explanation:
Method 1
The given logic circuit can be analyzed by determining the output at each stage.
  • The outputs of the three initial NAND gates are: \[\overline{P\,Q}, \quad \overline{Q\,R}, \quad \text{and} \quad \overline{P\,R}\]
  • From the above figure: \[X = \overline{\overline{P\,Q} \cdot \overline{Q\,R}} = \overline{\overline{P\,Q}} + \overline{\overline{Q\,R}} = P\,Q + Q\,R\]
  • The inverted value \(\overline{X}\) is then combined with the third NAND gate's output: \[Y = \overline{\overline{X} \cdot \overline{P\,R}} = \overline{\overline{X}} + \overline{\overline{P\,R}} = X + P\,R\]
  • Substituting the expression for \(X\): \[Y = P\,Q + Q\,R + P\,R\]
This expression represents a 3-input majority function, which outputs a \(1\) whenever two or more inputs are \(1\).
Method 2
Using the bubble-shifting technique, the NAND-NAND structure can be simplified:
  • Pushing the output bubbles of the input NAND gates to the inputs of the subsequent gates converts them into active-low OR gates.
  • The circuit directly reduces to a sum-of-products form: \[Y = P\,Q + Q\,R + P\,R\]
\[\boxed{\text{(B) two or more of the inputs } P, Q, R \text{ are ``1''}}\]
Key points
  • The Boolean expression \(Y = P\,Q + Q\,R + P\,R\) defines a majority gate or the Carry output (\(C_{out}\)) of a Full Adder.

questions.question:
An 8085 assembly language program is given below. Assume that the carry flag is initially unset. The content of the accumulator after the execution of the program is
MVI A, 07H
RLC
MOV B, A
RLC
RLC
ADD B
RRC
questions.explanation:
The program is executed instruction by instruction starting with the initial conditions. The carry flag (\(\text{CY}\)) is initially \(0\).
  1. MVI A, 07H
    This moves the hexadecimal value \(07\text{H}\) immediately into the Accumulator (Register \(A\)). In 8-bit binary: \[A = 0000\,0111_2\]
  2. RLC
    This instruction stands for Rotate Accumulator Left. Every single bit in Register \(A\) shifts left by one position. The leftmost bit (\(\text{D}_7\)) leaves its position and loops around to fill the rightmost empty spot (\(\text{D}_0\)), and it also copies itself into the Carry flag (\(\text{CY}\)). \[A = 0000\,1110_2 = 0\text{E H}, \quad \text{CY} = 0\]
  3. MOV B, A
    This copies the current contents of Register \(A\) straight into Register \(B\). \[B = 0000\,1110_2 = 0\text{E H}\]
  4. RLC, RLC
    We rotate the bits of Register \(A\) left twice. \[A = 0011\,1000_2 = 38\text{H}, \quad \text{CY} = 0\]
  5. ADD B
    This adds the binary value inside Register \(B\) to the current value inside Register \(A\) and stores the final result right back in Register \(A\) (\(A = A + B\)): \[\begin{array}{rcc} 0011\,1000_2 & \quad & (38\text{H}) \\ + \,\, 0000\,1110_2 & \quad & (0\text{E H}) \\ \hline 0100\,0110_2 & \quad & (4 6\text{H}) \end{array}\] Now, \(A = 0100\,1110_2\).
  6. RRC
    This stands for Rotate Accumulator Right. Every bit in Register \(A\) moves right by one position. The rightmost bit (\(\text{D}_0\)) leaves its spot, loops around to fill the leftmost open space (\(\text{D}_7\)), and copies itself into the Carry flag (\(\text{CY}\)). \[A = \mathbf{0}010\,0011_2, \quad \text{CY} = 0\]
Converting the final binary sequence \(0010\,0111_2\) into standard hex notation gives: \[0010_2 = 2, \quad 0111_2 = 7 \implies A = 23\text{H}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C) } 23\text{H}}\]
Key points
  • RLC (Rotate Left): Moves every bit left. \(\text{D}_7\) goes to \(\text{D}_0\) and also copies into the Carry flag (\(\text{CY}\)).
  • RRC (Rotate Right): Moves every bit right. \(\text{D}_0\) goes to \(\text{D}_7\) and also copies into the Carry flag (\(\text{CY}\)).
  • ADD r: Executes binary addition between the target register and the accumulator (\(A = A + r\)).

questions.question: The differential equation \[100\dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{dt}^2} - 20\dfrac{\text{dy}}{\text{dt}} + y = x(t)\] describes a system with an input \(x(t)\) and an output \(y(t)\). The system, which is initially relaxed, is excited by a unit step input. The output \(y(t)\) can be represented by the waveform
questions.explanation: Given the differential equation for the system: \[100 \frac{d^{2}y}{dt^{2}} - 20 \frac{dy}{dt} + y = x(t)\] Taking the Laplace transform on both sides (assuming zero initial conditions): \[100s^{2}Y(s) - 20sY(s) + Y(s) = X(s)\] \[G(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} = \frac{1}{100s^{2} - 20s + 1} = \frac{1}{(10s - 1)^{2}}\] For a unit step input \(x(t) = u(t)\), \(X(s) = \frac{1}{s}\). The output \(Y(s)\) is: \[Y(s) = \frac{1}{s(10s - 1)^{2}}\] The poles of the system are located at: \[s = 0, \frac{1}{10}, \frac{1}{10}\] Since the closed-loop poles \(s = 0.1\) lie on the RHS of the \(s\)-plane, the system is unstable. An unstable system's step response will grow without bound over time. Among the given options in the reference figure, only option (A) represents an unstable, unbounded waveform.

questions.question: The root locus plot for a system is given below. The open-loop transfer function corresponding to this plot is given by
questions.explanation:
• Zeros: There is a visible open-loop zero at \(s = -1\).
  • Poles on the real axis: There are poles at \(s = 0\) and \(s = -2\).
  • Behavior at \(s = -3\): The root locus branch on the real axis originates from \(s = -3\) and moves in both directions (to the left towards \(-\infty\) and to the right towards the break-away point). For a branch to move out in both directions from a single point on the real axis, there must be a multiple pole at that location. Therefore, there are \(2\) poles located at \(s = -3\).
Thus, the overall open-loop transfer function is given by: \[\boxed{(B) \ \ G(s)H(s) = K \dfrac{(s + 1)}{s(s + 2)(s + 3)^2}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Do not overlook the direction arrows near \(s = -3\). Mistaking it for a single pole would lead to an incorrect count of branches and asymptotes.

questions.question: An analog signal is band-limited to \(4\ \text{kHz}\), sampled at the Nyquist rate and the samples are quantized into \(4\) levels. The quantized levels are assumed to be independent and equally probable. If we transmit two quantized samples per second, the information rate is
questions.explanation: Theory: When all quantization levels are equally probable, the information contained in each sample is equal to the entropy of the source. Since there are \(4\) quantization levels and all are equiprobable, \[H = \log_2 4 = 2 \text{ bits/sample}.\]Given that the transmission rate is \[r=2 \text{ samples/sec},\]the information rate is \[R=rH.\]Substituting the values, \[R = 2 \times 2 = 4 \text{ bits/sec}.\]Therefore, \[\boxed{(D) R=4 \text{ bits/sec} }\]

questions.question: A message signal \(m(t)=\cos 2000\pi t+4\cos 4000\pi t\) modulates the carrier \(c(t)=\cos 2\pi f_ct\) where \(f_c=1\text{MHz}\) to produce an AM signal. For demodulating the generated AM signal using an envelope detector, the time constant \(RC\) of the detector circuit should satisfy
questions.explanation:
Theory: For proper envelope detection, the detector time constant must be much larger than the carrier period and much smaller than the message period. The design condition for an envelope detector is\[\frac{1}{f_c}\ll RC\ll\frac{1}{f_{m,\max}}.\]Here,\[f_c=1~\text{MHz},\]and the highest message frequency is \[f_{m,\max}=2~\text{kHz},\]since\[m(t)=\cos 2000\pi t+4\cos 4000\pi t.\]Therefore,\[\frac{1}{f_c} =\frac{1}{10^6} =1~\mu\text{s},\]and\[\frac{1}{f_{m,\max}} =\frac{1}{2000} =0.5~\text{ms}.\]Hence, \[\boxed{(B) 1~\mu\text{s}\ll RC<0.5~\text{ms}.}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Always use the highest message frequency \(f_{m,\max}\), not the lowest frequency component.
  • Do not confuse the carrier period with the carrier frequency.
  • Remember the envelope detector condition: \[\frac{1}{f_c}\ll RC\ll\frac{1}{f_{m,\max}}.\]
  • The factor \(4\) multiplying the second cosine affects only its amplitude, not its frequency.

questions.ref: Coordinate Geometry & Maxwell's Equation - Basics Q1
questions.question: A current sheet \(\vec{J} = 10\hat{u}_y\text{ A/m}\) lies on the dielectric interface \(x = 0\) between two dielectric media with \(\varepsilon_{r1} = 1, \mu_{r1} = 1\) in Region-1 (\(x < 0\)) and \(\varepsilon_{r2} = 2, \mu_{r2} = 2\) in Region-2 (\(x > 0\)). If the magnetic field in Region-1 at \(x = 0^-\) is \(\vec{H}_1 = 3\hat{u}_x + 30\hat{u}_y\text{ A/m}\), the magnetic field in Region-2 at \(x = 0^+\) is [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
The magnetic field boundary relations at the interface of two media are given by the continuity of the normal component of magnetic flux density and the discontinuity of the tangential component of magnetic field intensity.For magnetic field boundary relations: \[\vec{B}_{n1} = \vec{B}_{n2}\] \[\text{and} \quad \vec{H}_{t1} - \vec{H}_{t2} = -\vec{J}_{s} \times \hat{a}_{n}\]Assuming \(x\) is the normal component: \[B_{x1} = B_{x2}\] \[\mu_{1} H_{x1} = \mu_{2} H_{x2}\]Substituting the given values: \[1 \times 3 = 2 \times H_{x2}\] \[H_{x2} = 1.5\]Now, considering the tangential boundary condition:\[\vec{H}_{t1} - \vec{H}_{t2} = -10 \hat{u}_{y} \times \hat{u}_{x} = +10 \hat{u}_{z}\] \[\vec{H}_{t2} = 30 \hat{u}_{y} - 10 \hat{u}_{z}\]Combining the normal and tangential components, the total magnetic field intensity in region 2 is:\[\vec{H}_{2} = 1.5 \hat{u}_{x} + 30 \hat{u}_{y} - 10 \hat{u}_{z} \, \text{A/m}\]\[\boxed{(A) :\vec{H}_{2} = 1.5 \hat{u}_{x} + 30 \hat{u}_{y} - 10 \hat{u}_{z} \, \text{A/m}}\]
Key points
  • The normal component of \(\vec{B}\) is always continuous across a boundary: \(B_{n1} = B_{n2}\).
  • The tangential component of \(\vec{H}\) is discontinuous by an amount equal to the surface current density: \(\vec{H}_{t1} - \vec{H}_{t2} = -\vec{K} \times \hat{a}_{n}\).
  • Magnetic field intensity and flux density are related by \(\vec{B} = \mu \vec{H}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Pay close attention to the direction of the unit normal vector and the sign convention in the cross product for tangential components.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The electric and magnetic fields for a TEM wave of frequency \(14 \text{ GHz}\) in a homogeneous medium of relative permittivity \(\varepsilon_r\) and relative permeability \(\mu_r = 1\) are given by \[\vec{E} = E_p e^{j(\omega t - 280 \pi y)} \hat{u}_z \text{ V/m}\] \[\vec{H} = 3 e^{j(\omega t - 280 \pi y)} \hat{u}_x \text{ V/m}\]Assuming the speed of light in free space to be \(3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\), intrinsic impedance of free space to be \(120\pi\), the relative permittivity \(\varepsilon_r\) of the medium and the electric field amplitude \(E_p\) are
questions.explanation: Given the electric and magnetic field expressions for a plane wave: \[\vec{E} = E_{p} e^{j(\omega t - 280\pi y)} \hat{U}_{z} \text{ V/m}\] \[\vec{H} = 3 e^{j(\omega t - 280\pi y)} \hat{U}_{x} \text{ A/m}\] The phase constant \(\beta\) is identified from the exponent: \[\beta = 280\pi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\] \[\therefore \lambda = \frac{1}{140} \text{ m}\] The velocity of the wave in the medium is given by \(v = f\lambda\). Assuming a frequency \(f = 14 \times 10^{9} \text{ Hz}\): \[v = 14 \times 10^{9} \times \frac{1}{140} = 1 \times 10^{8} \text{ m/s}\] The velocity in a non-magnetic medium (\(\mu_{r} = 1\)) is related to the relative permittivity \(\epsilon_{r}\) by: \[v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r} \mu_{r}}} \implies 1 \times 10^{8} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{\sqrt{1 \times \epsilon_{r}}}\] \[\therefore \epsilon_{r} = 9\] The intrinsic impedance \(\eta\) of the medium is the ratio of the electric field amplitude \(E_{p}\) to the magnetic field amplitude \(H_{p}\): \[\eta = \frac{E_{p}}{H_{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\epsilon}} = \sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0} \times 1}{\epsilon_{0} \times 9}} = \frac{1}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\epsilon_{0}}}\] Given \(\sqrt{\mu_{0}/\epsilon_{0}} = 120\pi \text{ }\Omega\) and \(H_{p} = 3 \text{ A/m}\): \[\frac{E_{p}}{3} = \frac{1}{3} \times 120\pi\] \[\therefore E_{p} = 120\pi\] \[\boxed{(D): E_{p} = 120\pi,\epsilon_{r} = 9 }\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A transmission line of characteristic impedance \(50\ \Omega\) is terminated in a load impedance \(Z_L\). The VSWR of the line is measured as \(5\) and the first of the voltage maxima in the line is observed at a distance of \(\lambda/4\) from the load. The value of \(Z_L\) is
questions.explanation: Given the Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (\(\text{VSWR}\)) as \(5\): \[\text{VSWR} = \frac{1 + |\Gamma|}{1 - |\Gamma|} = 5\] \[1 + |\Gamma| = 5 - 5|\Gamma|\] \[6|\Gamma| = 4 \implies |\Gamma| = \frac{2}{3}\] Thus, the reflection coefficient \(\Gamma = \pm \frac{2}{3}\). Since the maximum voltage \(V_{max}\) is located at \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\) from the load, the minimum voltage \(V_{min}\) occurs at the load itself. The phase of the reflection coefficient \(\Gamma\) is determined by the position of \(V_{max}\): \[2\beta x_{max} = 2n\pi + \theta\] Substituting \(\beta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\) and \(x_{max} = \frac{\lambda}{4}\): \[2 \cdot \left( \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{\lambda}{4} \right) = \theta \implies \theta = \pi\] Since \(\Gamma = |\Gamma|e^{j\theta} = \frac{2}{3}e^{j\pi} = -\frac{2}{3}\). Now, using the relationship between \(\Gamma\) and the load impedance \(Z_{L}\) (with \(Z_{o} = 50\,\Omega\)): \[\Gamma = \frac{Z_{L} - Z_{o}}{Z_{L} + Z_{o}}\] \[-\frac{2}{3} = \frac{Z_{L} - 50}{Z_{L} + 50}\] \[-2(Z_{L} + 50) = 3(Z_{L} - 50)\] \[-2Z_{L} - 100 = 3Z_{L} - 150\] \[5Z_{L} = 50\] \[Z_{L} = 10\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{(A):10}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A transmission line of characteristic impedance \(50\ \Omega\) is terminated by a \(50\ \Omega\) load. When excited by a sinusoidal voltage source at \(10\ \text{GHz}\), the phase difference between two points spaced \(2\ \text{mm}\) apart on the line is found to be \(\pi/4\) radians. The phase velocity of the wave along the line is
questions.explanation:
The phase difference between two points on a transmission line separated by a path difference is given by the relation: \[\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} (\Delta x)\] Given the phase difference \(\Delta\phi = \frac{\pi}{4}\) and path difference \(\Delta x = 2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\), we find the wavelength \(\lambda\): \[\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} (2 \times 10^{-3})\] \[\lambda = 8 \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 16 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\] With the frequency \(f = 10\,\text{GHz} = 10 \times 10^{9}\,\text{Hz}\), the phase velocity \(v\) of the wave along the line is calculated as: \[v = f\lambda\] \[v = (10 \times 10^{9}\,\text{Hz}) \times (16 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m})\] \[v = 160 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m/s} = 1.6 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\] \[\boxed{(C):1.6 \times 10^{8}}\]
Key points
  • The propagation constant \(\beta\) is related to wavelength by \(\beta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Mixing up units like GHz or mm during calculation.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The modes in a rectangular waveguide are denoted by \(\text{TE}_{mn}/\text{TM}_{mn}\) where '\(m\)' and '\(n\)' are the eigen numbers along the larger and smaller dimensions of the waveguide respectively. Which one of the following statements is true?
options: The \(\text{TM}_{10}\) mode of the waveguide does not exist.
The \(\text{TE}_{10}\) mode of the waveguide does not exist.
The \(\text{TM}_{10}\) and the \(\text{TE}_{10}\) modes both exist and have the same cut-off frequencies.
The \(\text{TM}_{10}\) and the \(\text{TE}_{01}\) modes both exist and have the same cut-off frequencies.
questions.explanation:
In a rectangular waveguide, the existence of specific modes is governed by the boundary conditions imposed by the conducting walls. The modal indices \(m\) and \(n\) determine the number of half-sinusoidal variations of the fields in the \(x\) and \(y\) directions, respectively.
  • TE\(_{mn}\) modes (Transverse Electric): These modes exist for all values of \(m\) and \(n\) except the case where \(m=0\) and \(n=0\) simultaneously. This is because a field configuration where both \(m=0\) and \(n=0\) results in a uniform field that cannot satisfy the boundary conditions (it leads to a zero field everywhere).
  • TM\(_{mn}\) modes (Transverse Magnetic): For these modes to exist, both indices \(m\) and \(n\) must be non-zero (i.e., \(m \geq 1\) and \(n \geq 1\)). If either \(m\) or \(n\) is zero, the boundary conditions for the longitudinal electric field component \(E_{z}\) are violated, resulting in a trivial solution (\(E_{z}=0\)).
\[\boxed{(A):\text{The $\text{TM}_{10}$ mode of the waveguide does not exist.}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the complex pointing vector \(\vec{P}\) for the power radiated by a point source in an infinite homogenous and lossless medium. \(\text{Re}(\vec{P})\) denotes the real part of \(\vec{P}\), \(S\) denotes a spherical surface whose center is at the point source, and \(\hat{n}\) denotes the unit surface normal on \(S\). Which of the following statements is true?
options: \(\text{Re}(\vec{P})\) remains constant at any radial distance from the source.
\(\text{Re}(\vec{P})\) increases with increasing radial distance from the source.
\(\iint_{s} \text{Re}(\vec{P}) \cdot \hat{n} \, dS\) remains constant at any radial distance from the source.
\(\iint_{s} \text{Re}(\vec{P}) \cdot \hat{n} \, dS\) decreases with increasing radial distance from the source.
questions.explanation: The power density \(P_{d}\) of a point source radiating uniformly in all directions decreases as it propagates because the total power \(P\) is distributed over an increasingly larger surface area \(A\) of a sphere centered at the source. For a sphere of radius \(r\), the surface area is \(A = 4\pi r^2\). Thus, the power density is given by: \[P_{d} = \frac{P}{A} = \frac{P}{4\pi r^2}\] This equation shows that the power density is inversely proportional to the square of the distance (\(P_{d} \propto 1/r^2\)). Since the product of the power density and the area is the total power \(P\), which remains constant for an isotropic source, we have: \[P = P_{d} \times A = \text{constant}\] \[\boxed{(C): \iint_{S} \text{Re}(\vec{P}) \cdot \hat{n} \, dS = \text{constant}, \text{ at any radial distance from the source.}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate word or phrase from the options given below to complete the following sentence. The environmentalists hope the lake to its pristine condition.
questions.explanation:
The sentence structure requires an infinitive complement following the transitive matrix verb hope to indicate a future goal or intended action.
  • The standard idiomatic construction is hope + to-infinitive. Therefore, "hope to restore the lake" is the only grammatically valid choice.
\[\boxed{\text{C: to restore}}\]
Key points
  • Verb Complementation: Certain English verbs, such as hope, decide, refuse, and manage, strictly govern an infinitive complement rather than a gerund or prepositional phrase.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Avoid using prepositional alternatives like "in restoring" or "in the restoration of" which violate the standard structural syntax of the verb hope.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the word from the options given below that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the given word: Polemical
questions.explanation:
The word "Polemical" describes an aggressive, strongly critical, or disputatious attack on someone else's opinions or principles. Evaluating the choices:
  • imitative: Tending to copy or mimic.
  • conciliatory: Intended or likely to placate, pacify, or bring about agreement and harmony. This is the exact semantic antonym of being aggressively argumentative.
  • truthful: Honest or factually accurate.
  • ideological: Based on a system of ideas or ideals.
\[\boxed{\text{B: conciliatory}}\]
Key points
  • Antonym Identification: When dealing with argumentative or conflict-oriented vocabulary, look for descriptors that convey peace-making or compromising intents as your baseline antonyms.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse an ideological focus with active polemics; an ideology can be presented without initiating personal written or verbal disputes.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate word from the options given below to complete the following sentence: Despite the mixture's nature, we found that by lowering its temperature in the laboratory we could dramatically reduce its tendency to vaporize.
questions.explanation:
The context sets up an inverse relationship using the keyword "Despite". The phrase "by lowering its temperature... we could dramatically reduce its tendency to vaporize" implies that the mixture naturally turns into vapor very rapidly or easily under normal conditions.
  • acerbic: Sharp, sour, or bitter in taste or character.
  • resilient: Able to withstand or recover quickly from difficult conditions.
  • volatile: Evaporating rapidly; easily passing off in the form of vapor. This fits the physical context perfectly.
  • heterogeneous: Composed of parts of different kinds.
\[\boxed{\text{C: volatile}}\]
Key points
  • Physical Chemistry Modifiers: A substance that displays an intense baseline tendency to transform from a liquid phase to a gas phase is chemically defined as being highly volatile.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate words from the options given below to complete the following sentence: Because she had a reputation for , we were surprised and pleased when she greeted us so .
questions.explanation:
The introductory word "Because" indicates that her action matched her preexisting reputation. The following phrase "we were surprised and pleased" establishes that her choice of greetings was highly positive and pleasant.
  • To be pleased by a greeting, it must be warm and courteous. Evaluating the available options based on the answer key, the correct pair requires matching structural context where her typical negative reputation was surprisingly subverted by a positive greeting layout.
  • A baseline reputation for querulousness (habitually complaining or whining) makes a warm, welcoming greeting like affably a pleasant surprise.
\[\boxed{\text{D: querulousness ...... affably}}\]
Key points
  • Textual Inversion Signals: When "surprised and pleased" modifies a behavior, the reputation field and the behavioral adverb field should ideally feature contrasting situational polarities to generate a complete subversion of expectations.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: In order to develop to full potential, a baby needs to be physically able to respond to the environment. It can be inferred from the passage that
options: Full physical potential is needed in order for a baby to be able to respond to the environment.
It is necessary for a baby to be able to physically respond to the environment for it to develop its full potential.
Response to the environment of physically able babies needs to be developed to its full potential.
A physically able baby needs to develop its full potential in order to respond to its environment.
questions.explanation:
Let us break down the exact logical proposition structure presented in the prompt:
  • Premise: "In order to develop to full potential, a baby needs to be physically able to respond to the environment."
  • This follows the classical conditional requirement format: \(A\) is necessary for \(B\) (\(B \implies A\)).
  • Therefore, being physically able to respond to the environment (\(A\)) is an essential requirement or a necessary condition for a baby to achieve its full potential (\(B\)).
Evaluating the choices:
  • Option A: Inverts the logic by claiming full potential is needed to respond, which is structurally backwards.
  • Option B: Correctly restates the premise using explicit logical constraints: it clarifies that responding to the environment is a necessary condition for developing full potential.
  • Option C and Option D: Warp the conditional links by converting necessary conditions into absolute sufficient statements.
\[\boxed{\text{B: It is necessary for a baby to be able to physically respond to the environment for it to develop its full potential.}}\]
Key points
  • Necessary Conditions vs Sufficient Conditions: The structural qualifier phrase "In order to achieve X, Y is required" frames Y as an indispensable necessity. It does not mean Y alone is automatically sufficient to guarantee X, but without Y, X cannot occur.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the word from the options given below that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the given word: Deference
questions.explanation:
The word "Deference" means polite submission, respect, or esteem shown toward another individual's judgment, wishes, or authority. Evaluating the options:
  • aversion: A strong dislike or disinclination toward something.
  • resignation: Acceptance of an undesirable but inevitable situation.
  • suspicion: A feeling or thought that something is possible, likely, or true.
  • contempt: The feeling that a person or a thing is beneath consideration, worthless, or deserving of utter scorn. This is the exact semantic antonym of showing respect or deference.
\[\boxed{\text{D: contempt}}\]
Key points
  • Antonym Matching: When identifying an antonym for an attitude of high respect or politeness (deference), select a trait that communicates open disrespect or disregard (contempt).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not choose aversion; though negative, it describes avoidance or dislike rather than active disrespect or lack of esteem.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate word(s) from the options given below to complete the following sentence: We lost confidence in him because he never the grandiose promises he had made.
questions.explanation:
The sentence explains a loss of confidence due to an unfulfilled commitment.
  • The phrasal verb deliver on means to fulfill, satisfy, or carry out an expectation, pledge, or promise.
  • Option A ("delivered") is transitive and typically requires the direct object to immediately follow it if used in this sense (e.g., "he never delivered the promises"). With the noun phrase positioned downstream, "delivered on" is structurally required.
  • Option D ("reneged on") means to go back on a promise. Since the modifier "never" is already present, using "never reneged on" would mean he kept his promises, contradicting the first clause.
\[\boxed{\text{B: delivered on}}\]
Key points
  • Phrasal Verb Complementation: Pledges, oaths, and promises are idioms handled by the phrasal combination deliver on.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence below. in the frozen wastes of Arctic takes special equipment.
questions.explanation:
The sentence tests infinitive vs. gerund usage as a subject noun phrase modifying a predicate that takes an object complement.
  • The official answer key marks option A as correct. The phrase "To survive in the frozen wastes of Arctic takes special equipment" uses an initial infinitival clause to establish a purpose-driven or conditional subject baseline.
  • While the gerund "Surviving" (Option B) is common in descriptive speech, the infinitive "To survive" highlights the targeted objective or necessary action required by the equipment.
\[\boxed{\text{A: To survive}}\]
Key points
  • Infinitival Subjects: An infinitive verb string (to + verb) can act directly as the structural nominal subject of a sentence, framing an ultimate goal or prerequisite condition.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate word from the options given below to complete the following sentence: The of evidence was on the side of the plaintiff since all but one witness testified that his story was correct.
questions.explanation:
The sentence context provides that "all but one witness testified that his story was correct," which indicates an overwhelming volume of supportive statements favoring the plaintiff.
  • paucity: Scarcity or a small, insufficient quantity.
  • propensity: An inclination or natural tendency to behave in a particular way.
  • preponderance: A superiority in weight, power, importance, or strength of evidence; being greater in number or quantity. This matches the context of having nearly all witnesses supportive.
  • accuracy: The quality or state of being correct or precise.
\[\boxed{\text{C: preponderance}}\]
Key points
  • Legal Evidentiary Terms: The legal standard "preponderance of evidence" refers directly to the weight of evidence being greater on one side than on the other.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate word(s) from the options given below to complete the following sentence. I contemplated Singapore for my vacation but decided against it.
questions.explanation:
The sentence tests verb complementation patterns for the transitive matrix verb contemplate.

questions.question: If \(m\) students require a total of \(m\) pages of stationery in \(m\) days, then 100 students will require 100 pages of stationery in
questions.explanation:
We can solve this problem using the unitary method by evaluating the rate of resource consumption per student. Step 1: Understand the baseline rate data
Given that \(m\) students require a total of \(m\) pages of stationery over a span of \(m\) days, the work rate formula is: \[\text{Pages required} \propto \text{Number of students} \times \text{Number of days}\] \[\text{Pages} = k \times \text{Students} \times \text{Days}\] Using the initial parameters to find the constant \(k\): \[m = k \times m \times m \implies k = \dfrac{1}{m}\] Step 2: Apply the rate constant to the new scenario Let \(D\) be the number of days required by \(100\) students to use \(100\) pages of stationery: \[100 = \left(\dfrac{1}{m}\right) \times 100 \times D\] \[100 = \dfrac{100D}{m} \implies D = m \text{ days}\] \[\boxed{\text{D: } m \text{ days}}\]
Key points
  • Joint Variation Rate Layouts: Time required is directly proportional to the total workload (pages) and inversely proportional to the operating workforce size (students): \[\dfrac{\text{Students}_1 \times \text{Days}_1}{\text{Pages}_1} = \dfrac{\text{Students}_2 \times \text{Days}_2}{\text{Pages}_2}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not blindly jump to an option like "100 days" due to superficial pattern matching with the numerical constants; always process the underlying inverse time mechanics.

questions.question:
The number of solutions for the following system of inequalities is \[\begin{aligned}
        X_1 &\ge 0 \\
        X_2 &\ge 0 \\
        X_1 + X_2 &\le 10 \\
        2X_1 + 2X_2 &\ge 22
    \end{aligned}\]
questions.explanation:
We are given a system of linear inequalities with variables bounded in the first quadrant: \[\begin{aligned} 1) \quad &X_1 \ge 0 \\ 2) \quad &X_2 \ge 0 \\ 3) \quad &X_1 + X_2 \le 10 \\ 4) \quad &2X_1 + 2X_2 \ge 22 \implies 2(X_1 + X_2) \ge 22 \implies X_1 + X_2 \ge 11 \end{aligned}\] Let us evaluate inequalities (3) and (4) simultaneously:
  • Inequality (3) bounds the sum to a maximum ceiling of 10: \(X_1 + X_2 \le 10\).
  • Inequality (4) demands that the sum must be at least 11: \(X_1 + X_2 \ge 11\).
Since a real number value cannot be simultaneously less than or equal to 10 while being greater than or equal to 11 (\(11 \le X_1 + X_2 \le 10\)), these constraints are mutually exclusive. No overlapping feasibility region exists. Therefore, the number of solutions for the system is exactly 0. \[\boxed{\text{A: 0}}\]
Key points
  • Feasible Region Nullity: In linear programming models, if two constraint half-spaces display parallel boundary thresholds facing in opposite directions without overlap, the solution set is null.

questions.question: In a class of 300 students in an M.Tech programme, each student is required to take at least one subject from the following three: M600: Advanced Engineering Mathematics C600: Computational Methods for Engineers E600: Experimental Techniques for Engineers The registration data for the M.Tech class shows that 100 students have taken M600, 200 students have taken C600, and 60 students have taken E600. What is the maximum possible number of students in the class who have taken all the above three subjects?
questions.explanation:
Let the total number of students be \(N = 300\). We organize the data using set theory definitions:
  • \(n(M) = 100\) (Students taking M600)
  • \(n(C) = 200\) (Students taking C600)
  • \(n(E) = 60\) (Students taking E600)
Every single student is required to take at least one subject, meaning the union of the sets equals the entire class size: \[n(M \cup C \cup E) = N = 300\] Using the standard set inclusion-exclusion principle expansion for three sets: \[n(M \cup C \cup E) = n(M) + n(C) + n(E) - [n(M \cap C) + n(C \cap E) + n(M \cap E)] + n(M \cap C \cap E)\] Substitute the known values into the equation: \[300 = 100 + 200 + 60 - \sum n(\text{Pairs}) + n(M \cap C \cap E)\] \[300 = 360 - \sum n(\text{Pairs}) + n(M \cap C \cap E)\] \[\sum n(\text{Pairs}) - n(M \cap C \cap E) = 60 \quad \text{--- (1)}\] To find the *maximum possible value* of students taking all three subjects, let \(x = n(M \cap C \cap E)\). We rewrite equation (1) as: \[\sum n(\text{Pairs}) = 60 + x\] By principle bounding constraints, any student counted in all three subjects is inherently counted within each of the individual overlapping pairs: \[n(M \cap C) \ge x, \quad n(C \cap E) \ge x, \quad n(M \cap E) \ge x \implies \sum n(\text{Pairs}) \ge 3x\] Substitute our equation link into this inequality constraint: \[\begin{aligned} 60 + x &\ge 3x \\ 60 &\ge 2x \\ x &\le 30 \end{aligned}\] Thus, the maximum possible number of students who have taken all three subjects is 30. \[\boxed{\text{B: 30}}\]
Key points
  • Set Intersection Optimization: Maximizing the primary triple intersection region requires minimizing structural waste across individual non-overlapping dual-set pairs down to their baseline limits.

questions.question: Three sisters (R, S, and T) received a total of 24 toys during Christmas. The toys were initially divided among them in a certain proportion. Subsequently, R gave some toys to S which doubled the share of S. Then S in turn gave some of her toys to T, which doubled T's share. Next, some of T's toys were given to R, which doubled the number of toys that R currently had. As a result of all such exchanges, the three sisters were left with equal number of toys. How many toys did R have originally?
questions.explanation:
Let the number of toys originally held by sisters R, S, and T be represented by variables \(r, s,\) and \(t\) respectively. The absolute total number of toys is constant throughout all steps: \[r + s + t = 24 \text{ toys}\] At the end of all transactions, the three sisters are left with an equal number of toys: \[\text{Final toys per sister} = \dfrac{24}{3} = 8 \text{ toys}\] We solve this problem by working backwards step-by-step from the final state:
  • End State: \([R, S, T] = [8, 8, 8]\)
  • Reverse Step 3 (T doubled R's toys): R had \(8 \div 2 = 4\) toys. T gave away 4, so T had \(8 + 4 = 12\) toys. State: \([4, 8, 12]\)
  • Reverse Step 2 (S doubled T's toys): T had \(12 \div 2 = 6\) toys. S gave away 6, so S had \(8 + 6 = 14\) toys. State: \([4, 14, 6]\)
  • Reverse Step 1 (R doubled S's toys): S had \(14 \div 2 = 7\) toys. R gave away 7, so R had \(4 + 7 = 11\) toys. State: \([11, 7, 6]\)
Thus, R originally had exactly 11 toys. \[\boxed{\text{C: 11}}\]
Key points
  • Inversion Analysis: Finite transactional loops where cumulative volume remains constant are solved fastest by starting at the final equilibrium state and applying inverse arithmetic operations.

The absolute performance contribution of each independent factor is calculated by multiplying its score by its standardized coefficient: \[\text{Contribution} = \text{Score} \times \text{Coefficient}\] Let us evaluate the contribution metrics for each category: \[\begin{aligned} \text{Contribution}_{\text{ Outcome}} &= 7 \times 0.8 = 5.6 \\ \text{Contribution}_{\text{ Tangibles}} &= 4 \times 0.4 = 1.6 \\ \text{Contribution}_{\text{ Reliability}} &= 5 \times 0.7 = 3.5 \\ \text{Contribution}_{\text{ Responsiveness}} &= 6 \times 0.6 = 3.6 \\ \text{Contribution}_{\text{ Empathy}} &= 5 \times 0.6 = 3.0 \\ \text{Contribution}_{\text{ Assurance}} &= 7 \times 0.5 = 3.5 \end{aligned}\] Step 1: Calculate the overall sum of all contributions
\[\text{Total Quality Score} = 5.6 + 1.6 + 3.5 + 3.6 + 3.0 + 3.5 = 20.8\] Step 2: Identify the factor with the lowest contribution

questions.question: If \((2y+1)/(y+2) < 1\), then which of the following alternatives gives the CORRECT range of \(y\)?
questions.explanation:
Given the rational inequality expression: \[\dfrac{2y + 1}{y + 2} < 1\] Step 1: Rearrange the inequality to compare with zero Subtract 1 from both sides: \[\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2y + 1}{y + 2} - 1 &< 0 \\[1.5ex] \dfrac{(2y + 1) - (y + 2)}{y + 2} &< 0 \\[1.5ex] \dfrac{y - 1}{y + 2} &< 0 \end{aligned}\] Step 2: Find critical points and analyze intervals The critical boundary roots where the numerator or denominator equals zero are: \[y = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad y = -2\] Using the sign chart method (wavy curve method) across the partitioned intervals:
  • For \(y > 1\): Both \((y-1) > 0\) and \((y+2) > 0 \implies \text{Positive } (+)\)
  • For \(-2 < y < 1\): \((y-1) < 0\) but \((y+2) > 0 \implies \text{Negative } (-)\)
  • For \(y < -2\): Both \((y-1) < 0\) and \((y+2) < 0 \implies \text{Positive } (+)\)
Since we require the expression to be strictly less than zero (\(< 0\)), the valid interval is \(-2 < y < 1\). \[\boxed{\text{B: } -2 < y < 1}\]
Key points
  • Rational Inequalities Rule: Never cross-multiply by variable terms like \((y + 2)\) across an inequality sign, as the variable's sign is unknown and could reverse the inequality direction. Always transfer all terms to one side.

questions.question: A student attempted to solve a quadratic equation in \(x\) twice. However, in the first attempt, he incorrectly wrote the constant term and ended up with the roots as \((4, 3)\). In the second attempt, he incorrectly wrote down the coefficient of \(x\) and got the roots as \((3, 2)\). Based on the above information, the roots of the correct quadratic equation are
questions.explanation:
Let the correct quadratic equation format be \(x^2 + bx + c = 0\). Step 1: Extract valid parameters from the first attempt
In the first attempt, the student incorrectly wrote the constant term (\(c\)) but copied the coefficient of \(x\) (\(b\)) correctly.
  • Given roots: \((4,3)\)
  • The sum of the roots relates directly to \(b\): \[\text{Sum} = 4 + 3 = 7 = -b \implies b = -7\]
Step 2: Extract valid parameters from the second attempt
In the second attempt, the student incorrectly wrote the coefficient of \(x\) (\(b\)) but copied the constant term (\(c\)) correctly.
  • Given roots: \((3,2)\)
  • The product of the roots relates directly to \(c\): \[\text{Product} = 3 \times 2 = 6 = c \implies c = 6\]
Step 3: Construct the correct equation and find its true roots
Combining the true coefficients yields the original quadratic equation: \[x^2 - 7x + 6 = 0\] Factorizing by splitting the middle term: \[\begin{aligned} x^2 - 6x - x + 6 &= 0 \\ x(x - 6) - 1(x - 6) &= 0 \\ (x - 6)(x - 1) &= 0 \implies x = 6 \quad \text{or} \quad x = 1 \end{aligned}\] The actual roots of the correct quadratic equation are \((6,1)\). \[\boxed{\text{C: (6, 1)}}\]
Key points
  • Vieta's Formulas: For any quadratic equation \(x^2 + bx + c = 0\) with roots \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), the roots directly satisfy: \[\alpha + \beta = -b \quad \text{and} \quad \alpha\beta = c\]

questions.question: The variable cost (\(V\)) of manufacturing a product varies according to the equation \(V = 4q\), where \(q\) is the quantity produced. The fixed cost (\(F\)) of production of same product reduces with \(q\) according to the equation \(F = 100/q\). How many units should be produced to minimize the total cost (\(V+F\))?
questions.explanation:
We are given equations for variable cost \(V\) and fixed cost \(F\) relative to production quantity \(q\): \[V = 4q \quad \text{and} \quad F = \dfrac{100}{q}\] The total cost function \(C(q)\) is the sum of variable cost and fixed cost: \[C(q) = V + F = 4q + \dfrac{100}{q}\] Step 1: Differentiate with respect to production quantity \(q\)
To locate the production volume that minimizes total cost, take the first derivative and set it to zero: \[\dfrac{dC}{dq} = 4 - \dfrac{100}{q^2} = 0\] \[4 = \dfrac{100}{q^2} \implies 4q^2 = 100 \implies q^2 = 25 \implies q = 5 \quad (\text{since } q > 0)\] Step 2: Confirm the minimum with the second derivative
\[\dfrac{d^2C}{dq^2} = \dfrac{200}{q^3}\] Evaluating at \(q = 5\) yields \(\dfrac{200}{125} = 1.6 > 0\). Since the second derivative is positive, \(q = 5\) successfully minimizes total production cost. \[\boxed{\text{A: 5}}\]
Key points
  • Cost Optimization Minimums: Total cost optimizations can be solved dynamically by identifying where the marginal variable cost balances the changing marginal fixed asset costs.

Microbe S stands out as the most severe threat: it has the highest probability of overcoming human immunity (\(\approx 0.8\)) combined with the lowest lethal dose value (\(\approx 200 \text{ mg}\)). Therefore, it is the most dangerous microbe and should be targeted first. \[\boxed{\text{D: S}}\]
Key points
  • Inverse Metric Scales: Pay close attention to unit definitions on chart axes. When toxicity is measured as "amount required to destroy half of body mass," lower graph positions indicate much more dangerous and lethal agents.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Avoid assuming that higher positions on a graph always mean "more dangerous." Choosing microbe P because it sits at the top of the chart ignores the inverse definition of lethal dose mass.

questions.question: There are two candidates P and Q in an election. During the campaign, 40% of the voters promised to vote for P, and the rest for Q. However, on the day of election 15% of the voters went back on their promise to vote for P and instead voted for Q. 25% of the voters went back on their promise to vote for Q and instead voted for P. Suppose, P lost by 2 votes, then what was the total number of voters?
questions.explanation:
Let the total number of voters in the election be \(V\). Step 1: Set up the baseline campaign expectations
  • Promised votes for candidate P = \(40\%\) of \(V = 0.40V\)
  • Promised votes for candidate Q = Rest of the voters = \(60\%\) of \(V = 0.60V\)
Step 2: Account for the voting shifts on election day
  • \(15\%\) of P's promised voters switched to Q: \[\text{Loss for P} = 0.15 \times 0.40V = 0.06V\]
  • \(25\%\) of Q's promised voters switched to P: \[\text{Loss for Q} = 0.25 \times 0.60V = 0.15V\]
Step 3: Calculate final vote tally per candidate
\[\begin{aligned} \text{Final Votes for P} &= \text{Initial P} - \text{Switched from P} + \text{Switched from Q} \\ &= 0.40V - 0.06V + 0.15V = 0.49V \\[1.5ex] \text{Final Votes for Q} &= \text{Initial Q} - \text{Switched from Q} + \text{Switched from P} \\ &= 0.60V - 0.15V + 0.06V = 0.51V \end{aligned}\] Step 4: Solve for \(V\) using the margin constraint
We are given that candidate P lost by exactly 2 votes: \[\begin{aligned} \text{Votes for Q} - \text{Votes for P} &= 2 \\ 0.51V - 0.49V &= 2 \\ 0.02V &= 2 \\ V &= \dfrac{2}{0.02} = 100 \text{ voters} \end{aligned}\] \[\boxed{\text{A: 100}}\]
Key points
  • Double Shift Tracking: When modeling voter migration between two options, ensure that any volume deducted from one pool is explicitly added to the opposing pool to maintain total population integrity.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not misapply percentages by treating the \(15\%\) and \(25\%\) shifts as fractions of the global voter population \(V\); they are percentages of each candidate's local pool.

questions.question: Given that \(f(y) = |y| / y\), and \(q\) is any non-zero real number, the value of \(|f(q) - f(-q)|\) is
questions.explanation:
We are given the signum-style function definition: \[f(y) = \dfrac{|y|}{y}\] For any non-zero real number \(y\), the value of this function behaves as follows:
  • If \(y > 0\): \(f(y) = \frac{y}{y} = 1\)
  • If \(y < 0\): \(f(y) = \frac{-y}{y} = -1\)
We need to compute the absolute value expression for a non-zero real number \(q\): \[\text{Target} = |f(q) - f(-q)|\] Let us analyze the two possible cases for the sign of variable \(q\): Case 1: Assume \(q\) is positive (\(q > 0\))
If \(q > 0\), then \(-q < 0\). Evaluating our function values: \[f(q) = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad f(-q) = -1\] Substitute these values into our absolute target function: \[\text{Target} = |1 - (-1)| = |1 + 1| = |2| = 2\] Case 2: Assume \(q\) is negative (\(q < 0\))
If \(q < 0\), then \(-q > 0\). Evaluating our function values: \[f(q) = -1 \quad \text{and} \quad f(-q) = 1\] Substitute these values into our absolute target function: \[\text{Target} = |-1 - 1| = |-2| = 2\] In all possible cases, the expression evaluates to exactly 2. \[\boxed{\text{D: 2}}\]
Key points
  • Signum Function Properties: The function \(f(y) = \frac{|y|}{y}\) outputs the structural orientation sign of its input variable. Because \(q\) and \(-q\) must possess opposite signs, their corresponding function outputs are always pairs of \((1, -1)\) or \((-1, 1)\).

questions.question: The sum of \(n\) terms of the series \(4 + 44 + 444 + \dots\) is
questions.explanation:
We want to find the sum of \(n\) terms of the following arithmetic-geometric series: \[S_n = 4 + 44 + 444 + 4444 + \dots + \underbrace{444\dots4}_{n \text{ digits}}\] Step 1: Factor out the common digit 4
\[S_n = 4 \Big[ 1 + 11 + 111 + 1111 + \dots + \text{(term up to } n \text{ digits)} \Big]\] Step 2: Multiply and divide by 9 to create base-10 links
\[S_n = \dfrac{4}{9} \Big[ 9 + 99 + 999 + 9999 + \dots + \text{(term up to } n \text{ digits)} \Big]\] Step 3: Express each term as a power of 10 \[\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{4}{9} \Big[ (10^1 - 1) + (10^2 - 1) + (10^3 - 1) + \dots + (10^n - 1) \Big] \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{4}{9} \bigg[ \Big( 10^1 + 10^2 + 10^3 + \dots + 10^n \Big) - \Big( 1 + 1 + 1 + \dots + 1 \text{ ($n$ times)} \Big) \bigg] \end{aligned}\] Step 4: Sum the Geometric Progression (GP) series The first part forms a geometric progression with first term \(a = 10\) and common ratio \(r = 10\): \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 10^i = \dfrac{10(10^n - 1)}{10 - 1} = \dfrac{10^{n+1} - 10}{9}\] Substitute this expression back into our equation: \[\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{4}{9} \left[ \dfrac{10^{n+1} - 10}{9} - n \right] \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{4}{9} \left[ \dfrac{10^{n+1} - 10 - 9n}{9} \right] \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{4}{81} \left[ 10^{n+1} - 9n - 10 \right] \end{aligned}\] This result matches the formulation presented in Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C: } \dfrac{4}{81}[10^{n+1} - 9n - 10]}\]
Key points
  • Uniform Digit Series Expansion: Any repeating single-digit series of value \(d\) can be systematically transformed into a base-10 geometric progression using the following multiplier: \[\dfrac{d}{9}(10^k - 1)\]
